alternative: Accuracy plus problem difficulty, with no claim about what the opening means. Being in the rows depends on two things: T3 opens non-deliberatively, and step 100 still writes at least one quick, non-deliberative opening. Step 100 opens that way mainly on easy problems. On easy problems the plain base's answer-first T3 reply is also right fairly often, so t on these 60 rows is well above the 0.29 that non-deliberative T3 answers average over all 351 such problems (from result-1f98b0: T3 - T1 = -0.516 against T1 of about 0.82). If the opening flag carries no information about rightness within a problem, a non-deliberative step-100 sample is right at the step-100 model's own per-problem rate. Then D equals the accuracy-only value: step-100 per-sample right rate on easy problems (about 0.9) minus the base's T3 right rate on the same problems (about 0.55-0.6). That gap is about 0.3, inside [0.10, 0.38]. The step-100 model's general reliability gain over the plain base and the easiness of the selected problems are enough to produce the number.
computation: 1) From t1_t3_items-01/per_problem.json, take for each of the 500 problems the T3 v3 grade t_i (0/1) and T3's first 240 characters. From s0100_plain-01 (sample 0) and s0100_plain_s123-01 (samples 1-3), take each step-100 plain sample's v3 grade and first 240 characters. 2) Apply the flag rule of result-1f98b0 (no Okay/Hmm/Let me/Let's/Wait/First/Alright in the first 240 characters before any equation or 'Answer') only to pick the rows: T3 non-deliberative and at least 1 of the 4 step-100 samples non-deliberative (n should be 60). 3) Do not split the step-100 samples by their flag. For each row, a_i = (number of v3-right step-100 samples among all 4) / 4. 4) Predicted D_alt = mean over the rows of (a_i - t_i). This is the consequence's accuracy-only value. Under the covariate account it is the predicted value of D, and it should land at about 0.30.
